papers.title: Investigation of generalization to unseen audio generation models in audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction
papers.abstract: Text-to-audio generation (TTA) requires reliable evaluation of semantic alignment between generated audio and input text. Existing learning-based alignment-score prediction models have been evaluated only on audio generated by models included in the training data, leaving their generalization to unseen generation models unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the generalization of audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction models to unseen TTA models and introduce adversarial training using a generation-model classifier with a gradient reversal layer (GRL). Experimental results show that pretrained audio encoders capture generation-model-specific characteristics and that alignment-score prediction performance degrades on audio generated by unseen TTA models. Applying the GRL improves prediction performance in some settings, although its effectiveness in suppressing generation-model-specific information is limited.

papers.title: Bridging the Gap: Reconciling the Legal Recognition of Alternative Dispute Resolution with Institutional Implementation in Music Copyright Disputes in Tanzania
papers.abstract: The resolution of music copyright royalty disputes in Tanzania presents a legal paradox: while Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) is formally recognized across various statutes, its practical application remains fragmented and institutionally ineffective. The Copyright and Neighbouring Rights (Royalty Collection and Distribution) (Collective Management Organisations) Regulations, GN No. 211 of 2023, recognize amicable settlement and permit referral to independent ADR, yet disputes over royalty calculations, payment delays, and distribution formulas persist. This article argues that the primary challenge is not the absence of a legal framework, but the distance between legal recognition and institutional operationalization. Drawing on a doctrinal examination of the Tanzanian legal framework and a comparative analysis of Singapore’s integrated ADR model, the article demonstrates that the existing framework blurs the line between genuine ADR and administrative determination, subjects access to ADR to the discretionary gatekeeping of the collective management organizations, and fails to provide procedural clarity, confidentiality safeguards, or specialized expertise. By comparatively analyzing Singapore’s structured, institutionally supported mediation framework under the Intellectual Property (Dispute Resolution) Act 2019 and the Copyright (Collective Management Organisations) Regulations 2023, this article proposes targeted reforms. It concludes that Tanzania must move from mere statutory recognition to a coherent, dedicated ADR pathway that is independent, transparent, and legally predictable, thereby aligning with the constitutional right to property and the utilitarian imperative of a thriving creative economy.

papers.title: TigerTTS: Draft-Guided Multi-Frame Parallel Speech-Token Language Model for Fast and Robust Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Autoregressive speech-token language models enable high-quality TTS but suffer from latency growth with sequence length, word omission or repetition without explicit alignment, and fidelity limits from discrete codebooks. We present TigerTTS, a production-grade LLM TTS system built around a lightweight non-autoregressive NAR model. With explicit alignment, the NAR model drafts tokens for the entire utterance, which are refined frame-by-frame by a compact autoregressive LLM. The draft is aligned frame-for-frame with LLM targets and injected at the input, ensuring training-inference consistency. Leveraging its accuracy, the LLM predicts 12 tokens per step across 3 frames and 4 groups, while a conditional-total-correlation bound keeps parallel prediction nearly lossless. We use a codebook-free FSQ tokenizer with four parallel groups and about 1800 bps to avoid codebook collapse. The backbone keeps positional information only in input embeddings, enabling exact MLA weight absorption and a four-fold KV-cache reduction. Decoding uses CUDA Graphs with a graph-safe multinomial sampler. A Fast mode further reduces first-packet latency: the NAR generator acts as a prefix synthesizer with RTF 0.03, producing the first 500 ms before LLM decoding. With CUDA-Graph decoding, TigerTTS reaches RTF 0.05, about 20x real-time, on one GPU. Despite using a 0.15B backbone, it outperforms standard PyTorch inference of VoxCPM2 2B by 5x and CosyVoice 2 by 16x. TigerTTS achieves the lowest CER and WER on SEED, 1.09 and 1.67, and strong WER, NMOS, and speaker similarity on LibriSpeech test-clean, 2.22, 4.36, and 0.820. Fast-mode guided semantic tokens provide a well-aligned content prior, reducing dropped words, loops, and runaway generation without sacrificing speed.

papers.title: Evaluating Cine and Tagged MRI-to-Speech Synthesis with Complementary Metrics and MRI-Free Controls
papers.abstract: Relating tongue motion measured with dynamic MRI to the speech it produces could inform rehabilitation after glossectomy. Prior studies have translated cine or tagged MRI into log-mel spectrograms and used the two-dimensional Pearson correlation between predicted and recorded spectrograms (Corr2D) to quantify the acoustic information captured by each imaging modality. However, Corr2D has not been calibrated against MRI-free predictors that preserve basic acoustic structure. Our contribution is an evaluation framework for speech synthesis from cine MRI, tagged MRI and their combination; the synthesis network is held fixed. On identical leave-one-subject-out folds, we compare four trained input configurations with two MRI-free controls: a static mean-spectrum baseline and a time-aligned cohort template. Across 44 subjects (18 after glossectomy) producing two utterances, the cohort template, which never sees an MRI, reached a Corr2D of 0.745 and 0.664. The static baseline, which contains no timing, reached 87 to 89% of that score. No trained configuration outperformed the template on Corr2D, a cepstral distance or ESTOI; seven of the eight fell significantly short on Corr2D. For cine MRI this held across three positional encodings, an encoder temporal-attention module and a training objective matched to the metric. Cine and tagged MRI differed consistently within subjects, although the direction depended on the metric. Absolute Corr2D alone therefore does not show that a model recovers acoustics from the MRI. The two controls are a reusable method: any study can compute them from its own training recordings, so a model's margin over them measures what its images contribute.

papers.title: Speech-based MCI screening and photo-driven reminiscence dialogue modules toward an integrated community cognitive health platform
papers.abstract: The growing prevalence of Alzheimer disease and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) amid global aging calls for cognitive health care that is both accessible and emotionally engaging: conventional screening tools require trained professionals in clinical settings and may be susceptible to the “white coat effect,” while existing digital cognitive training programs often fail to sustain engagement among older adults. This study developed and separately evaluated two complementary modules for community-based cognitive health support—a lightweight speech-based MCI screening module and a Korean-language vision-language model (VLM)-based photo-driven reminiscence dialogue module. The MCI screening module employs a KoBERT-based text classifier operating on automatic speech recognition transcriptions of structured conversational dialogue, with domain adversarial training applied for cross-paradigm robustness across four task types. Two Korean elderly speech corpora were constructed (KorMCI-MP and KorMCI-CD), with a curated subset deposited in DementiaBank as the Korean Kang Corpus, the first large-scale Korean MCI speech dataset accessible to the international research community. The reminiscence training module fine-tunes KoLLaVA-v1.5-Synatra-7b on a visual instruction following dataset derived from approximately 30,000 era-specific historical Korean photographs, using psychiatrist-informed prompts covering eight memory focus categories; an animated digital human avatar delivers questions via text-to-speech. In laboratory evaluation, accuracy was 87.5% on the combined four-paradigm KorMCI-MP/CD corpus. On the single-paradigm KorMCI-CD corpus, accuracy was 94.4% with manual transcriptions and 91.7% with ASR-generated transcriptions. Community-based field validation with 90 participants at local dementia care centers and senior welfare facilities achieved 85.6% accuracy, 72.0% sensitivity, and 90.8% specificity relative to screening-defined K-MMSE/CDR labels. The fine-tuned VLM generated structured multi-turn reminiscence dialogues spanning eight memory focus categories, in marked contrast to the generic scene descriptions of the pretrained baseline, with the prompt framework and representative question sets reviewed by a consulting psychiatrist. In a structured usability evaluation with 20 community-dwelling older adults, all completed the training tasks without dropout, and emotional satisfaction was the highest-rated of six usability domains (3.67/5). Together with the controlled-access Korean Kang Corpus, these findings support the technical feasibility and preliminary acceptability of two complementary modules for community-based cognitive health support. Their closed-loop integration and clinical effectiveness remain to be evaluated prospectively.

papers.title: An AI and IOT-Based Voice Assistant for Smart Multilingual Conversational E-Commerce
papers.abstract: Conventional e-commerce platforms primarily rely on graphical user interfaces that require users to navigate through multiple screens, enter search queries, examine product listings, and manually manage shopping carts. These interaction requirements can create difficulties for elderly individuals, visually impaired users, people with limited digital literacy, regional-language speakers, and users who prefer hands-free interaction. This paper proposes an Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT)-based multilingual voice assistant for conversational e-commerce. The proposed system is designed as a Raspberry Pi-based personal shopping assistant that enables users to search for products, compare alternatives, receive recommendations, and manage a local shopping cart through natural speech. The system captures spoken commands through a microphone and converts them into text using Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). An AI-based natural language processing module identifies user intent and extracts relevant product requirements, including product category, budget, brand, and preferred features. Product-related requests are processed through an external Product Search Application Programming Interface (API), which retrieves relevant product information. The retrieved information is processed to provide comparisons and personalized recommendations based on the user's stated preferences. The proposed system supports English, Hindi, Telugu, and Gujarati, depending on the language coverage of the selected speech recognition and synthesis services. Text-to-Speech (TTS) technology generates spoken responses, while an LCD provides supplementary visual information, including product names, prices, recommendations, and shopping cart details. The architecture integrates Raspberry Pi 4 or Raspberry Pi 5, microphone, speaker, LCD, Wi-Fi connectivity, speech processing services, a Large Language Model (LLM), product search APIs, and Python-based cart management. The system focuses on shopping assistance rather than autonomous purchasing and does not process payments or complete merchant checkout. This paper presents the proposed architecture, literature review, implementation methodology, evaluation framework, limitations, and future enhancements. The performance of the proposed system will be established through experimental testing after implementation. Key Words— Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things, Conversational Commerce, Raspberry Pi, Voice Assistant, Multilingual Speech Recognition, Large Language Model, Product Recommendation, Accessibility, Speech-to-Text, Text-to-Speech.

papers.title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
papers.abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (Instruct-TTS) renders a target transcript in the manner described by a free-form natural-language instruction, and a good rendition must succeed on three fronts at once: following the instruction, pronouncing the transcript correctly, and sounding natural. Reinforcement learning has become the standard way to post-train such generative models toward human preferences, and TTS systems increasingly adopt it. When the three objectives are optimized together under a single scalar reward, typically with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), training tends to be unstable: the objectives compete, and the shared update drifts toward whichever one is easiest to improve, producing a seesaw among them. We instead adapt on-policy distillation (OPD), which fuses several single-objective teachers by matching their velocity fields on the student's own rollouts. Realizing this for Instruct-TTS first calls for a sound reward on each axis, which we analyze carefully: a distilled Qwen-Omni proxy for the costly Gemini judge, dialect-free data for the WER reward, and DNSMOS in place of the language-biased UTMOS. We then train three single-objective teachers with GRPO and fuse them with OPD, routing each rollout to the instruction-following or WER teacher by its data domain and letting every rollout additionally follow the MOS teacher for quality. This lets instruction following and intelligibility improve together without a trade-off, but the quality target conflicts with instruction following, so following it additively reintroduces the seesaw. We therefore propose conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction that opposes the primary objective before fusing, and show that it markedly reduces the instruction-following/quality trade-off. The fused model improves over scalar-reward GRPO on all three objectives at once.

papers.title: Accurate, Label-Efficient, and Edge-Deployable Sound Event Detection: Methods for Complex Acoustic Scenes
papers.abstract: Sound event detection must answer two questions at once: what is sounding, and for how long. This requirement separates sound event detection from clip-level tagging and explains why a detector can perform well on classification while still failing in time-sensitive applications. This review examines the tension between localization quality, learning from incomplete labels, and execution on constrained hardware. Convolutional recurrent networks established useful temporal baselines, whereas attention models and differentiable frame-to-event mappings have improved long-range context and boundary handling. Weak-label disentanglement, pseudo-label training, and separation-guided detection reduce annotation demands, but each introduces biases that remain difficult to measure. Lightweight conformers and spiking networks make edge operation increasingly realistic, although reported efficiency is rarely tied to a complete hardware workload. Across these lines, the field lacks a common basis for deciding whether an F1 gain justifies extra annotation, computation, or complexity. This review argues for evaluation that reports localization, robustness, and resource cost together, and identifies open-set operation, continual adaptation, and reproducible benchmarking as priorities.

papers.title: Forensic Voice Comparison in the Era of Automatic Speaker Recognition: Methods, Validation, Mismatch Conditions, and Evaluative Interpretation
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Forensic voice comparison (FVC) evaluates whether speech recordings are more consistent with propositions asserting a common speaker origin or different speaker origins. Modern forensic speech science has systematically evolved from impressionistic, categorical conclusions toward transparent, empirically validated systems that integrate digital signal processing, statistical modeling, score calibration, and evaluative likelihood-ratio (LR) reporting. While automatic speaker recognition (ASR) provides highly efficient, objective, and reproducible measurements, its raw output is not self-validating: a complete forensic evaluation system encompasses the recordings, signal preprocessing, acoustic feature extraction, speaker modeling, similarity scoring, relevant population definition, score-to-likelihood-ratio calibration, and formal reporting. Methods: This narrative review examines the evolution and operational integration of auditory-acoustic-phonetic (AAP) methods alongside modern deep learning architectures, focusing on state-of-the-art neural embeddings including x-vectors, ECAPA-TDNN, and raw waveform architectures. Results: It synthesizes recent empirical validations under realistic casework conditions, examining the impact of complex technical and physiological mismatch factors (such as facial coverings, exertion, and channel degradation), while clearly delineating human speaker comparison from synthetic speech detection and anti-spoofing countermeasures targeting voice cloning. Furthermore, it explores multi-modal information fusion combining acoustic embeddings with authorship attribution, evaluates relevant population selection strategies, and reviews empirical findings comparing human listener performance against automated systems. Conclusions: Grounded in institutional standards such as ENFSI methodological guidelines and ISO 21043 standards, this paper reinforces the principle that forensic voice results should be presented as the strength of evidence for explicitly formulated, mutually exclusive propositions rather than posterior probabilities of guilt or speaker identity.

Open models are now good enough to stand on their own, and what was missing is the studio around them: that is what we build, in the open. ## 30-Second Quickstart (Exact 1-Line `transformers` Drop-In)

Works across standard `transformers>=4.30` (zero breaking version constraints and zero `trust_remote_code`).

> **Important Threshold Note:** Default `0.50` argmax favors ultra-low false alarms on authentic human voices (`0.3%` real-speaker FPR on `Commercial TTS`), but yields conservative `15.4%` fake recall on clean studio commercial TTS (ElevenLabs/Kokoro/Hume). For high-recall commercial TTS screening, threshold `P(fake) >= 0.20` as shown below; keep `0.50` for ultra-low false-alarm call verification.

```bash
pip install transformers torch numpy librosa soundfile
```

```python
import numpy as np
from transformers import pipeline

# Exact 1-line drop-in replacement for mo-thecreator/Deepfake-audio-detection
# and MelodyMachine/Deepfake-audio-detection-V2 (id2label = {0: "fake", 1: "real"})
detector = pipeline("audio-classification", model="Tamarillo/voice-deepfake-guard-base")

# Self-contained 2.0s 16 kHz test buffer (replace with: wav, _ = librosa.load("call.wav", sr=16000, mono=True))
wav = np.zeros(2 * 16000, dtype=np.float32)

# Pass raw 16 kHz mono audio up to 4.0s (matches benchmark evaluation; no silence trimming required)
scores = detector({"array": wav[: 4 * 16000], "sampling_rate": 16000})
p_fake = next(s["score"] for s in scores if s["label"] == "fake")
verdict = "FAKE" if p_fake >= 0.20 else "REAL"  # tau=0.20 for high-recall screening; 0.50 for <1% real FPR
print(f"{verdict} | P(fake)={p_fake:.4f} | raw={scores}")
```

## Label Schema, Preprocessing & Operating Thresholds (`calibration.json`)

| Class ID | Label | Meaning |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| `0` | `fake` | Synthetic / TTS / zero-shot voice-cloned / voice-converted (spoof) speech. |
| `1` | `real` | Authentic human (bonafide) speech. |

- **Silence Trimming (Train vs. Inference):** Training trims leading/trailing silence (`librosa.effects.trim(wav, top_db=30)`) so models cannot learn dataset-specific padding shortcuts. **All benchmarks in Tables 1–2 run on raw, untrimmed `16 kHz` audio** (first `4.0s`), and inference snippets do not require silence trimming. For real telephony streams with long initial dead air (`>0.5s` silence before speech starts), run a lightweight VAD/trim before taking the `1s–4s` window.
- **Calibration ([`calibration.json`](calibration.json)) vs. OOD Raw Thresholds:** Validation temperature `T = 0.9838` (applied as `softmax(logits / T)`), validation EER = `0.28%`, calibrated ECE = `0.0260`. On our in-domain cross-attack validation split, class separation is near-complete, placing temperature-scaled `thr_val_5pct_fpr = 0.0100` and `thr_val_1pct_fpr = 0.0102` near `0.01`. For **out-of-domain commercial TTS screening**, we recommend thresholding raw uncalibrated `P(fake)` at **`τ = 0.15–0.20`** (high recall) or **`τ = 0.50`** (ultra-low `0.3%` real-speaker FPR), or calibrating `τ` on a small sample of your target voice channel.

## Benchmarks (4 Zero-Touch OOD Suites + Unseen-Attack `ASVspoof5` Eval + Streaming & Chinese OOD)

All 7 models were evaluated head-to-head on identical frozen `16 kHz` mono audio clips with **zero evaluation clips present in training**. Full reproducible data, training, and evaluation scripts are bundled in this repository: [`scripts/build_audio_data_v2.py`](scripts/build_audio_data_v2.py), [`scripts/train_audio_model.py`](scripts/train_audio_model.py), and [`scripts/eval_audio_suite.py`](scripts/eval_audio_suite.py). Bold marks the best value (or ties) in each column.

### Evaluation Protocol & Subsampling Details
- **Windowing & Preprocessing:** Table 1 scores the first **`4.0s`** (`64,000` samples at `16 kHz` mono) of every raw, **untrimmed** audio clip (`trim_sil=False`). Table 2 additionally scores `1.0s` and `2.0s` cropped windows on `Commercial TTS` and `ASVspoof2021_LA`.
- **Strict Zero-Touch vs. Unseen-Attack Test Split:** Four suites (`Commercial TTS`, `DFADD`, `In-The-Wild`, `ASVspoof2021_LA`) are **100% zero-touch OOD corpora** never seen during training. The fifth suite (`ASVspoof5` Eval) is the official held-out Track 1 test split (unseen speakers and unseen attacks `A17–A32`, strictly disjoint from `ASVspoof5` `train`/`dev` `A01–A16` used in training). We report **both** the **4-Suite Strict Zero-Touch OOD Mean** and the **5-Suite Public Mean**.
- **Dataset Sizes & Balanced Sampling:**
  - `ood_commercial_tts` (`garystafford/deepfake-audio-detection`, `CC-BY-4.0`): **full dataset (`n=1,866`)** — real YouTube human speech vs. ElevenLabs, Hume AI, Amazon Polly, Luvvoice, Speechify, and Kokoro.
  - `ood_dfadd_diffusion` (`SpeechAntiSpoofingBenchmarks/DFADD`, `MIT`): **full available streamed test set capped at 1,000/class (`n=1,755`, `seed=103`)** — 2024 Diffusion & Flow-Matching TTS (`GradTTS`, `Matcha-TTS`, `NaturalSpeech2`, `PFlow`, `ProDiff`).
  - `ood_in_the_wild` (`SpeechAntiSpoofingBenchmarks/InTheWild`, eval-only): **deterministic 50/50 balanced subset (`n=2,000`: 1,000 real / 1,000 fake, `seed=104`)** — Müller et al. (Interspeech 2022) public-figure deepfakes vs. interviews/podcasts (evaluation-only, never trained on).
  - `ood_asvspoof2021_la` (`SpeechAntiSpoofingBenchmarks/ASVspoof2021_LA`, `ODC-BY`): **deterministic 50/50 balanced subset (`n=2,000`: 1,000/1,000, `seed=102`)** — real VoIP / PSTN telephony codecs (`Opus`, `G.722`, `μ-law`, `a-law`, `GSM`). *(Note: `mo-thecreator` and `Gustking` trained on `ASVspoof2019_LA`, which shares `VCTK` speakers and attacks with `ASVspoof2021_LA`; Tamarillo never saw `ASVspoof2019_LA`.)*

## Honest Limitations & Where Baselines Win

1. **`ASVspoof2021_LA` Telephony Benchmark (`mo-thecreator` & `Gustking` win):** `mo-thecreator` (`0.50%` EER) and `Gustking` (`2.25%` EER) significantly outperform Tamarillo (`17.70%–26.35%` EER) on `ood_asvspoof2021_la`. Both incumbents trained on `ASVspoof2019_LA`, which shares `VCTK` source speakers and legacy `A07–A19` attack systems with `ASVspoof2021_LA`, whereas Tamarillo never saw `ASVspoof2019_LA` (and beats both incumbents by large margins on `ASVspoof5`, `Commercial TTS`, `DFADD`, and `In-The-Wild`).
2. **Conservative Default `@0.50` Recall on Studio Commercial TTS:** While `Tamarillo/voice-deepfake-guard-base` achieves `12.43%` EER (`0.943` AUC) on `Commercial TTS`, its raw softmax cutoff at `0.50` yields **`15.4%` fake recall at `0.3%` real-speaker FPR** (compared to `Gustking` `75.6%` recall at `16.4%` real FPR, and `mo-thecreator` `78.9%` recall at `26.2%` real FPR). Lower the decision threshold to **`τ = 0.15–0.20`** for high-recall commercial TTS screening, or calibrate on a small in-domain validation sample.
3. **Language Coverage & Zero-Touch Chinese Ordering (`small-en` > `base` on `DECRO`):** Although `base` uses the 128-language `XLS-R` backbone and fine-tunes on 5 languages (`en/de/fr/it/zh`), evaluation covers only English (5 suites) and zero-touch Chinese (`DECRO`); German, French, and Italian performance is currently unevaluated. On Chinese `DECRO`, English-only `small-en` (`2.38%` EER) and `tiny-en` (`5.19%`) outperformed `base` (`12.44%` EER) despite `base` training on `CFAD` Mandarin (likely due to recording/vocoder calibration shift between `CFAD` and `DECRO`).
4. **Duration Sensitivity & Defense-in-Depth:** Trained on `1.0s–4.0s` `16 kHz` mono segments; very short `1.0s` narrowband telephony clips (`ASVspoof2021_LA`) degrade substantially (`35.45%–39.90%` EER vs. `17.70%–26.35%` at `4.0s`). Prefer `2s–4s` windows for production calls, aggregate sliding windows on longer recordings, and pair acoustic forensics with speaker verification / liveness checks in high-stakes authentication.
5. **Quantization Availability:** FP16 ONNX is omitted across tiers due to ORT normalization parity failures, and INT8 is omitted on `small-en` after failing our `<= 0.08` probability parity gate.

## 30-Second Quickstart (Exact 1-Line `transformers` Drop-In)

Works across standard `transformers>=4.30` (zero breaking version constraints and zero `trust_remote_code`).

> **Important Threshold Note:** Default `0.50` argmax favors ultra-low false alarms on authentic human voices (`0.3%` real-speaker FPR on `Commercial TTS`), but yields conservative `27.8%` fake recall on clean studio commercial TTS (ElevenLabs/Kokoro/Hume). For high-recall commercial TTS screening, threshold `P(fake) >= 0.20` as shown below; keep `0.50` for ultra-low false-alarm call verification.

```bash
pip install transformers torch numpy librosa soundfile
```

```python
import numpy as np
from transformers import pipeline

# Exact 1-line drop-in replacement for mo-thecreator/Deepfake-audio-detection
# and MelodyMachine/Deepfake-audio-detection-V2 (id2label = {0: "fake", 1: "real"})
detector = pipeline("audio-classification", model="Tamarillo/voice-deepfake-guard-small-en")

# Self-contained 2.0s 16 kHz test buffer (replace with: wav, _ = librosa.load("call.wav", sr=16000, mono=True))
wav = np.zeros(2 * 16000, dtype=np.float32)

# Pass raw 16 kHz mono audio up to 4.0s (matches benchmark evaluation; no silence trimming required)
scores = detector({"array": wav[: 4 * 16000], "sampling_rate": 16000})
p_fake = next(s["score"] for s in scores if s["label"] == "fake")
verdict = "FAKE" if p_fake >= 0.20 else "REAL"  # tau=0.20 for high-recall screening; 0.50 for <1% real FPR
print(f"{verdict} | P(fake)={p_fake:.4f} | raw={scores}")
```

- **Silence Trimming (Train vs. Inference):** Training trims leading/trailing silence (`librosa.effects.trim(wav, top_db=30)`) so models cannot learn dataset-specific padding shortcuts. **All benchmarks in Tables 1–2 run on raw, untrimmed `16 kHz` audio** (first `4.0s`), and inference snippets do not require silence trimming. For **out-of-domain commercial TTS screening**, we recommend thresholding raw uncalibrated `P(fake)` at **`τ = 0.15–0.20`** (high recall) or **`τ = 0.50`** (ultra-low `0.3%` real-speaker FPR), or calibrating `τ` on a small sample of your target voice channel.

## Honest Limitations & Where Baselines Win

1. **`ASVspoof2021_LA` Telephony Benchmark (`mo-thecreator` & `Gustking` win):** `mo-thecreator` (`0.50%` EER) and `Gustking` (`2.25%` EER) significantly outperform Tamarillo (`17.70%–26.35%` EER) on `ood_asvspoof2021_la`. Both incumbents trained on `ASVspoof2019_LA`, which shares `VCTK` source speakers and legacy `A07–A19` attack systems with `ASVspoof2021_LA`, whereas Tamarillo never saw `ASVspoof2019_LA` (and beats both incumbents by large margins on `ASVspoof5`, `Commercial TTS`, `DFADD`, and `In-The-Wild`).
2. **Conservative Default `@0.50` Recall on Studio Commercial TTS:** While `Tamarillo/voice-deepfake-guard-small-en` achieves `16.88%` EER (`0.914` AUC) on `Commercial TTS`, its raw softmax cutoff at `0.50` yields **`27.8%` fake recall at `0.3%` real-speaker FPR** (compared to `Gustking` `75.6%` recall at `16.4%` real FPR, and `mo-thecreator` `78.9%` recall at `26.2%` real FPR). Lower the decision threshold to **`τ = 0.15–0.20`** for high-recall commercial TTS screening, or calibrate on a small in-domain validation sample.
3. **English-Trained Scope & Cross-Lingual Behavior:** This tier was fine-tuned exclusively on English speech. While it transfers strongly to zero-touch Chinese `DECRO` (`2.38%` EER on `small-en`, `5.19%` on `tiny-en`), non-English performance on other languages is unevaluated.
4. **Duration Sensitivity & Defense-in-Depth:** Trained on `1.0s–4.0s` `16 kHz` mono segments; very short `1.0s` narrowband telephony clips (`ASVspoof2021_LA`) degrade substantially (`35.45%–39.90%` EER vs. `17.70%–26.35%` at `4.0s`). Prefer `2s–4s` windows for production calls, aggregate sliding windows on longer recordings, and pair acoustic forensics with speaker verification / liveness checks in high-stakes authentication.
5. **Quantization Availability:** FP16 ONNX is omitted across tiers due to ORT normalization parity failures, and INT8 is omitted on `small-en` after failing our `<= 0.08` probability parity gate.

## Benchmarks (4 Zero-Touch OOD Suites + Unseen-Attack `ASVspoof5` Eval + Streaming & Chinese OOD)

All 7 models were evaluated head-to-head on identical frozen `16 kHz` mono audio clips with **zero evaluation clips present in training**. Full reproducible data, training, and evaluation scripts are bundled in this repository: [`scripts/build_audio_data_v2.py`](scripts/build_audio_data_v2.py), [`scripts/train_audio_model.py`](scripts/train_audio_model.py), and [`scripts/eval_audio_suite.py`](scripts/eval_audio_suite.py). Bold marks the best value (or ties) in each column.

### Evaluation Protocol & Subsampling Details
- **Windowing & Preprocessing:** Table 1 scores the first **`4.0s`** (`64,000` samples at `16 kHz` mono) of every raw, **untrimmed** audio clip (`trim_sil=False`). Table 2 additionally scores `1.0s` and `2.0s` cropped windows on `Commercial TTS` and `ASVspoof2021_LA`.
- **Strict Zero-Touch vs. Unseen-Attack Test Split:** Four suites (`Commercial TTS`, `DFADD`, `In-The-Wild`, `ASVspoof2021_LA`) are **100% zero-touch OOD corpora** never seen during training. The fifth suite (`ASVspoof5` Eval) is the official held-out Track 1 test split (unseen speakers and unseen attacks `A17–A32`, strictly disjoint from `ASVspoof5` `train`/`dev` `A01–A16` used in training). We report **both** the **4-Suite Strict Zero-Touch OOD Mean** and the **5-Suite Public Mean**.
- **Dataset Sizes & Balanced Sampling:**
  - `ood_commercial_tts` (`garystafford/deepfake-audio-detection`, `CC-BY-4.0`): **full dataset (`n=1,866`)** — real YouTube human speech vs. ElevenLabs, Hume AI, Amazon Polly, Luvvoice, Speechify, and Kokoro.

## ONNX Parity & Same-Machine 4-Thread x86 CPU Latency (`1.0s / 2.0s / 4.0s` Audio)

Hardware: GCP `a2-highgpu-1g` (Intel Xeon Cascade Lake @ 2.20 GHz, AVX-512, 4 ORT threads, `bs=1`, median p50 ms over 15 timed runs after 3 warmups, `RTF = latency / clip_duration`). For apples-to-apples CPU timing, incumbents (which ship **no official ONNX**) were exported locally to FP32 ONNX on the exact same machine:
- `mo-thecreator/Deepfake-audio-detection` (`94.6M`, `378.5 MB` FP32): **`50.34 ms`** @ `1.0s` (`RTF 0.0503`) | **`90.25 ms`** @ `2.0s` | **`169.01 ms`** @ `4.0s`.
- `Gustking/wav2vec2-large-xlsr-deepfake-audio-classification` (`315.7M`, `1,263.3 MB` FP32): **`140.42 ms`** @ `1.0s` (`RTF 0.1404`) | **`238.64 ms`** @ `2.0s` | **`468.66 ms`** @ `4.0s`.

- **Parity Protocol & Quantization Caveats:** Parity was verified against PyTorch FP32 across `n=16` held-out validation clips spanning `1.0s`, `2.0s`, and `4.0s` windows; full 5-suite EER benchmarks in Table 1 were run on PyTorch FP32 weights. FP16 ONNX is omitted across tiers because ORT CPU normalization checks did not pass our numeric parity gate.

## Training Recipe & Upstream-Audited Data Provenance

Trained end-to-end (**unfrozen 7-layer raw-waveform CNN frontend** with `0.5×` differential LR + native `use_weighted_layer_sum=True` across all transformer layers + focal cross-entropy `gamma=1.2`, label smoothing `0.03`, EMA `0.996`, validation-only EER selection) on **`35,779` strictly domain-matched real/fake clips** (`val=2,892` cross-attack validation set) with leading/trailing silence trimming (`top_db=30`) and **real `ffmpeg` production codecs** (`libopus` 12–16 kbps, `g722`, `pcm_mulaw` 8 kHz, `pcm_alaw` 8 kHz, `libmp3lame` 48 kbps, `aac` 32 kbps) applied symmetrically 50/50 across real and fake speech. Every training source carries verified commercially permissive upstream provenance:

1. **ASVspoof 5 Official `train` (`A01–A08`) & `dev` (`A09–A16`)** (`jungjee/asvspoof5`, `ODC-BY`, upstream `MLS` `CC-BY-4.0`) — 100% disjoint speakers and attacks from `ASVspoof5` `eval` (`A17–A32`).
2. **CD-ADD** (`SpeechAntiSpoofingBenchmarks/CD-ADD`, `CC-BY-4.0`) — matched `LibriTTS` & `TED Talks` genuine speech vs. `OpenVoice`, `VALL-E`, `WhisperSpeech`, `YourTTS`, and `Seamless`.
3. **CVoiceFake (small, English split)** (`SpeechAntiSpoofingBenchmarks/CVoiceFake_small`, `CC-BY-4.0`, upstream Mozilla `CommonVoice` `CC0-1.0`).
4. **Fresh 2025–2026 Zero-Shot Voice Clones & Speech-to-Speech VC (Matched 1:1 with Real Domains):** Synthesized on A100 using `Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-Base` (Jan 2026, `Apache-2.0`), `ResembleAI/chatterbox` Turbo (2025, `MIT`), and `ChatterboxVC` speech-to-speech voice conversion (2025, `MIT`) conditioned 1:1 on real spontaneous meeting (`edinburghcstr/ami`, `CC-BY-4.0`), 8 kHz banking call-center (`PolyAI/minds14`, `CC-BY-4.0`), and read (`openslr/librispeech_asr`, `CC-BY-4.0`) voices.

---

## Honest Limitations & Where Baselines Win

1. **`ASVspoof2021_LA` Telephony Benchmark (`mo-thecreator` & `Gustking` win):** `mo-thecreator` (`0.50%` EER) and `Gustking` (`2.25%` EER) significantly outperform Tamarillo (`17.70%–26.35%` EER) on `ood_asvspoof2021_la`. Both incumbents trained on `ASVspoof2019_LA`, which shares `VCTK` source speakers and legacy `A07–A19` attack systems with `ASVspoof2021_LA`, whereas Tamarillo never saw `ASVspoof2019_LA` (and `Tamarillo/voice-deepfake-guard-tiny-en` beats both incumbents by large margins on `ASVspoof5`, `Commercial TTS`, and `DFADD`, while trailing `mo-thecreator` (`10.60%`) and `Gustking` (`15.05%`) on `In-The-Wild` (`15.80%`)).
2. **Conservative Default `@0.50` Recall on Studio Commercial TTS:** While `Tamarillo/voice-deepfake-guard-tiny-en` achieves `16.72%` EER (`0.899` AUC, `65.3%` `TPR@5%FPR`) on `Commercial TTS`, its raw softmax cutoff at `0.50` yields **`33.3%` fake recall at `0.8%` real-speaker FPR** (compared to `Gustking` `75.6%` recall at `16.4%` real FPR, and `mo-thecreator` `78.9%` recall at `26.2%` real FPR). Lower the decision threshold using [`calibration.json`](calibration.json) or calibrate on a small target-channel sample when prioritizing recall on commercial TTS.
3. **English-Trained Scope & Cross-Lingual Behavior:** This tier was fine-tuned exclusively on English speech. While it transfers strongly to zero-touch Chinese `DECRO` (`2.38%` EER on `small-en`, `5.19%` on `tiny-en`), non-English performance on other languages is unevaluated.
4. **Duration Sensitivity & Defense-in-Depth:** Trained on `1.0s–4.0s` `16 kHz` mono segments; very short `1.0s` narrowband telephony clips (`ASVspoof2021_LA`) degrade substantially (`35.45%–39.90%` EER vs. `17.70%–26.35%` at `4.0s`). Prefer `2s–4s` windows for production calls, aggregate sliding windows on longer recordings, and pair acoustic forensics with speaker verification / liveness checks in high-stakes authentication.
5. **Quantization Scope & INT8 Benchmark Caveat:** FP16 ONNX is omitted across tiers due to ORT normalization parity failures, and INT8 is omitted on `small-en` after failing our `<= 0.08` probability parity gate. Full 5-suite EER benchmarks in Table 1 were evaluated on PyTorch FP32 weights; INT8 parity was checked on `n=16` held-out clips (`100%` argmax agreement at `0.50`, `max Δp = 0.03458` on `tiny-en` / `0.00092` on `base`), so full-suite INT8 EER is not separately reported (use `onnx/model.onnx` FP32 for exact `<= 0.00001` probability parity).

Learn more about the family: https://tokenai.llc/projects/replica-preview ## Model Details | Property | Value | |---|---| | **Model type** | English Text-to-Speech (TTS) with reference-based voice cloning | | **Architecture** | Autoregressive T3 + S3Gen | | **Parameters** | 746,425,718 tensor elements (~0.7B) | | **Primary language** | English | | **Output sample rate** | 24 kHz | | **Voice inventory** | No fixed speaker catalog; speaker identity is conditioned by a reference recording | | **Model ID** | `replica-preview-0.7b-en` | | **Ownership** | TokenAI | The complete active inference path totals **746,425,718 parameters (~0.74B)**, reported publicly as **0.7B**. ## Capabilities - English text-to-speech generation. - Reference-based voice cloning with a consenting speaker reference. - Natural conversational speech generation. - Support for short and long English utterances. - Reproducible generation with configurable temperature and sampling settings. ## Voice Cloning Provide a clean reference recording from one consenting speaker, preferably longer than five seconds and with limited background noise. The reference conditions the generated speaker identity; it does not create a fixed speaker catalog. Voice similarity can vary with reference duration, recording quality, prosody, and text. Do not use generated speech to impersonate a person without authorization. ## Recommended Settings ```text temperature=0.8 top_p=0.95 top_k=1000 repetition_penalty=1.2 ``` These settings are the validated starting point for the current release. Adjust them only after checking intelligibility and speaker identity. ## Validation The current release was evaluated with regression comparisons, English voice-cloning stress samples, CPU/GPU inference measurements, clipping checks, and clean-directory loading. The evaluation did not establish a validated speaker-similarity score, so no unsupported similarity claim is made here. ## Audio Samples Audio samples are not hosted or displayed in this repository. Project page: https://tokenai.llc/projects/replica-preview ## About TokenAI **TokenAI** is an AI startup founded on May 10, 2025 by **Assem Sabry**. Our mission is to make advanced intelligence accessible and useful for everyone. Website: https://assem.one ## Contact TokenAI For inquiries, partnerships, or support, contact TokenAI at **info@tokenai.llc**. ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{replica_preview_07b_en_2026, title={Replica Preview 0.7B EN}, author={TokenAI}, year={2026}, url={https://huggingface.co/tokenaii/Replica-Preview-0.7B-EN} } ```

English words too.** Meet **Howard 0.6B**. It reads Burmese text aloud, including the English words, names and phrases we mix into everyday speech. Give it a few seconds of someone’s voice and the words they said, and it reads new text in that voice. *Sounding human is hard. Howard is just warming up.* ## Listen **Everyday Burmese**
ဒီနေ့ မိုးရွာလို့ အိမ်မှာ စာဖတ်နေပါတယ်။

ဒီနေ့ meeting ကို online ကနေ တက်ပါမယ်။
*“I’ll join today’s meeting online.”* ### Voice cloning Listen to the original speaker, then hear Howard read a different line in the same voice. Howard made the second clip on a Mac from the first clip and its transcript.
Reference recording · 4.4 s Howard reads new text

## What Howard does - **Burmese text-to-speech** — reads everyday Burmese aloud as 24 kHz mono audio. - **Burmese–English code-switching** — reads the English words inside a Burmese sentence as English. - **Voice cloning** — speaks new text in a voice learned from a short recording and its exact transcript. - **Runs on your own computer** — BF16 safetensors for PyTorch, 8-bit MLX for Apple silicon, and GGUF for qwentts.cpp. ## Use voices with permission Only clone a voice when you have the speaker’s permission. Don’t use Howard to impersonate a real person, to put words in someone’s mouth, or to mislead listeners about who is speaking.
